lesson.title: Doubling Down: The Octave as Audio's Favorite Frequency Unit
lesson.summary: An octave is a doubling of frequency, the same logarithmic idea as a decade but built around a factor of 2 instead of 10, and it is the unit musicians and audio engineers reach for by instinct.
lesson.body:
Just as a decade measures a tenfold change in frequency, an octave measures a twofold change: doubling a frequency moves it up exactly one octave. The word comes straight from music, where doubling the frequency of a note produces a note that sounds like the same note, but higher, the interval between a note and the eighth note above it on a standard scale. A 440 Hz concert A note, for instance, sits exactly one octave below 880 Hz and exactly one octave above 220 Hz, and this is not a coincidence of tuning, it is the literal definition of what makes two notes an octave apart. Going up two octaves from 440 Hz means doubling twice, 440 to 880 to 1760 Hz, and going up three octaves means doubling three times, reaching 3520 Hz, since each additional octave simply multiplies the previous frequency by another factor of 2.

The number of octaves between two frequencies f1 and f2 is found using a base 2 logarithm rather than base 10: number of octaves = log2(f2 divided by f1). Since most calculators do not have a dedicated log base 2 button, it is useful to know the conversion log2(x) = log10(x) divided by log10(2), where log10(2) is approximately 0.30103.

Worked example: consider a frequency range from 1000 Hz to 8000 Hz, a range that shows up often in tweeter and crossover specifications for loudspeakers. The ratio is f2/f1 = 8000/1000 = 8. Using the octave formula, number of octaves = log2(8) = 3, since 2 cubed equals 2 times 2 times 2 equals 8 exactly. So this range spans exactly 3 octaves. Checking this with the conversion formula as well: log10(8) is approximately 0.9031, and 0.9031 divided by 0.30103 is approximately 3.0, confirming the same answer both ways.

Octaves connect directly back to decades through the fixed conversion between decibels per decade and decibels per octave, since both describe the same underlying filter steepness, just measured against a different multiplying step. A slope of 20 dB per decade, the standard roll off rate of a first order filter mentioned earlier, converts to decibels per octave by multiplying by log10(2): 20 times 0.30103 is approximately 6.02 dB per octave, almost always rounded to the familiar figure of 6 dB per octave that audio engineers quote constantly. A second order filter's 40 dB per decade roll off similarly converts to about 12 dB per octave, and this 6 dB per octave per filter order pattern is one of the most frequently memorized numbers in audio electronics.

Octaves are preferred over decades specifically in audio work because human pitch perception is itself logarithmic in this base 2 sense, equal octave steps sound like equally spaced musical intervals regardless of where they fall in the frequency range, which is why graphic equalizers, spectrum analyzers, and loudspeaker crossover specifications are so often labeled in octaves or fractions of an octave, such as a 1/3 octave band, rather than in raw hertz or in decades.
